== Mathematical definition ==

Let $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{F}^n$ be a set, $+,\cdot$ be two [[binary operation]]s.

$(\mathbf{V},+,\cdot)$ is a '''vector space''' over $\mathbb{F}$ if:

1. Are defined operations
* of addition: $+:\mathbf{V} \times \mathbf{V} \to \mathbf{V}$
* of scalar multiplication: $\cdot: \mathbb{F} \times \mathbf{V} \to \mathbf{V}$

2. Are satisfied the properties
* Additive commutativity: $\forall \vec{u},\vec{v}\in\mathbf{V},\; \vec{u}+\vec{v}=\vec{v}+\vec{u}$;
* Associativity (vector addition, scalar multiplication): $\forall \vec{u},\vec{v},\vec{w}\in\mathbf{V},\;\forall a,b\in\mathbb{F},\; (\vec{u}+\vec{v})+\vec{w}=\vec{u}+(\vec{v}+\vec{w})\;\land\;(a\cdot b)\vec{v}=a\cdot(b\cdot \vec{v})$;
* Additive identity (vector): $\exists \vec 0\in\mathbf{V},\;\forall \vec{v}\in\mathbf{V},\; \vec 0+\vec{v}=\vec{v}$;
* Additive inverse: $\forall \vec{v}\in\mathbf{V},\;\exists \vec{w}\in\mathbf{V},\; \vec{v}+\vec{w}=0$;
* Multiplicative identity (scalar): $\exists 1_V \in \mathbf{V}: \forall \vec{v}\in\mathbf{V},\; 1_V \cdot \vec{v}=\vec{v}$;
* Distributivity: $\forall \vec{u},\vec{v}\in\mathbf{V},\;\forall a,b\in\mathbb{F},\; a\cdot(\vec{u}+\vec{v})=a\vec{u}+a\vec{v}\;\land\;(a+b)\cdot \vec{u}=a\cdot \vec{u}+b\cdot \vec{u}$.

<ref>{{#cite:Q1866}}</ref>

== Elementary properties ==

For vector space $V$ over $\mathbb{F}$:

=== The $\vec 0$ is unique ===

$$\exists!\,\vec 0\in V,\;\forall v\in V,\;\vec 0+v=v.$$

{{Hidden proof}}
Let $\vec 0,\vec 0_1\in V$ satisfy $\forall v\in V,\;\vec 0+v=v$ and $\forall v\in V,\;\vec 0_1+v=v$. Then

$$
\vec 0-\vec 0_1=\vec 0 \\
\vec 0 - \vec 0 = \vec 0_1 \\
\vec 0=\vec 0_1
$$

Hence $\vec 0=\vec 0_1$.
{{End hidden}}

=== The additive inverse for each vector is unique ===

$$\forall v\in V,\;\exists!\,w\in V,\;v+w=\vec 0.$$

{{Hidden proof}}
Let $w,w'\in V$ satisfy $v+w=\vec 0$ and $v+w'=\vec 0$. Then
$$w=w+\vec 0=w+(v+w')=(w+v)+w'=\vec 0+w'=w'.$$
Hence $w=w'$.
{{End hidden}}

=== Scalar $0$ mutiplies by any vector results in $\vec 0$ (the vector zero) ===

$$\forall v\in V,\;0v=\vec 0.$$

{{Hidden proof}}
For $v\in V$,
$$0v=(0+0)v=0v+0v.$$
Adding the additive inverse of $0v$, $-0v$, to both sides, we obtain
$$\vec 0=0v.$$
{{End hidden}}

=== Any scalar multiples of $\vec 0$ is $\vec 0$ ===

$$\forall a\in\mathbb{F},\;a\vec 0=\vec 0.$$

{{Hidden proof}}
For $a\in\mathbb{F}$,
$$a\vec 0=a(\vec 0+\vec 0)=a\vec 0+a\vec 0.$$
Adding the additive inverse of $a\vec 0$, $-a\vec 0$ to both sides, we obtain
$$\vec 0=a\vec 0.$$
{{End hidden}}

=== Scalar $-1$ multiples by any vector results in the additive inverse of the vector ===

$$\forall v\in V,\;(-1)v=-v.$$

{{Hidden proof}}
For $v\in V$,
$$v+(-1)v=1v+(-1)v=(1+(-1))v=0v=\vec 0,$$
which shows that $(-1)v$ is the additive inverse $-v$ of $v$.

<ref>{{#cite:Q1893}}</ref>
{{End hidden}}
